name: Female gaze / male gaze

card.summary: A framework for separating what women tend to find attractive in men from what other men judge as impressive, used to decide which looks traits to prioritise.
card.note: Borrowed from film and art theory; the looksmaxxing usage is a community adaptation.

quick.overview:
In looksmaxxing, 'female gaze' and 'male gaze' describe two different audiences for a man's appearance. Female gaze refers to the traits women are said to respond to when judging men, while male gaze refers to the traits men notice and rank in other men, such as height, frame, jawline and muscle mass. People use the split to decide which parts of their appearance to work on.

The terms come from film and art theory, where the male gaze describes women being depicted for a heterosexual male viewer. Looksmaxxing forums reversed and extended the idea to describe how each sex evaluates male looks. Scholarly work on the original concept exists; no study has tested the forum version directly.
quick.how: Members use the framework as a lens when choosing priorities: someone aiming at dating outcomes may weight traits they associate with the female gaze (facial harmony, grooming, style, a lean athletic build), while someone aiming at status among men may weight traits they associate with the male gaze (height, width, dominant features). Threads typically argue the two lists differ and compare ratings by each sex.
quick.risks: The framework is a community heuristic rather than a measured model, so the lists of traits attached to each gaze vary by poster and are disputed. Critics within the forums call parts of it coping; the academic literature on the original term links the male gaze to body shame and appearance anxiety in women.

lead: Female gaze and male gaze are paired terms that looksmaxxing communities use to separate two audiences for appearance. In the usual forum framing, the male gaze is what men notice and rank when they look at other men or at women, and the female gaze is what women respond to. People use the split to decide which traits to work on first: proponents say that a feature that impresses other men, such as height or a very muscular frame, is not always the one that draws women's interest, and that the reverse can also hold.[6][8][9]

The terms are borrowed from art and film theory. John Berger popularised the idea that Western art presents women as objects of men's looking in Ways of Seeing (1972), and Laura Mulvey formalised the 'male gaze' for cinema in her 1975 essay 'Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema'. Later theorists proposed a female gaze as a counter-perspective.[1][2][3] Looksmaxxing forums kept the vocabulary but changed its use, applying it to ratings of how people look rather than to how images are made. Threads on looksmax.org apply the pair to women's looks too, comparing a fashion-industry ideal with a type they describe as appealing to men.[6]

Within looksmaxxing the pair sits beside other framework vocabulary such as PSL ratings, mogging and the blackpill, which Wikipedia describes as part of an online culture that formed on early forums in the 2010s and spread on TikTok in the 2020s.[4][21] Forum members debate what each gaze consists of, whether rating scales reflect one or the other, and whether the female-gaze idea is a realistic guide or a coping narrative.[7][8][9][10][11] Psychology research examines the original concept, particularly how being looked at affects women, and research on mate preferences examines what women and men tend to prefer in male bodies and faces; no study has tested the looksmaxxing framework as such.[5][16][17]

chain: Separate what men notice from what women respond to
Pick the audience that matches your goal
Spend effort on the traits that audience weights
angle.text: People use the split to choose between, for example, grooming, style and facial harmony versus height and frame, depending on whether they want to appeal to women, to men, or both. It is a planning lens rather than a technique.

paras: In forum usage the two terms describe who is doing the judging. Members who talk about the female gaze mean the traits they believe women respond to when judging men or a given look, and members who talk about the male gaze mean the traits that other men notice, admire or compete over.[8][9] Threads that ask for definitions show that the terms are not fixed; posters supply their own lists, and the debate about what belongs on each list is a regular feature.[8][9]

The framework is used as a prioritising device. Someone aiming mainly at dating outcomes may focus on what they take to be female-gaze traits, such as facial harmony, grooming, skin, hair and a lean athletic build, while someone interested in status among men may weight height, shoulder width, muscularity and other features they count as male-gaze traits. Proponents describe this as a way of not spending effort on traits that the intended audience does not weight heavily.[11][13]

Wikipedia traces the philosophical idea of 'the gaze' to Jean-Paul Sartre's Being and Nothingness (1943), where being looked at turns a person into an object. John Berger's book and television series Ways of Seeing (1972) argued that Western art cast women as objects of men's looking and reinforced patriarchal norms, and Laura Mulvey's 1975 essay 'Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema', drawing on Freudian psychoanalysis, set out the male gaze as a feature of narrative film.[1]

Mulvey described three viewpoints in film, those of the camera, the spectator and the male characters, and coded looking as active and male and being looked at as passive and female.[1] The concept spread from film studies into art history, advertising and fashion criticism.[1]

Theorists including Griselda Pollock (1988), Lorraine Gamman (1989) and Mary Ann Doane (1999) examined how women view and resist the gaze, and the Wikipedia article on the female gaze describes it as a perspective of a female spectator, character or director that represents women as subjects with agency. It can be taken up by people of any gender.[1][2] The director Joey Soloway proposed in a 2016 masterclass the ideas of 'feeling seeing', the 'gazed gaze' and 'returning the gaze'.[2]

Scholars disagree about what the female gaze consists of. Natalie Perfetti-Oates (2015) analysed how films present male bodies for female viewers, and Caetlin Benson-Allott (2017) argued that television's female gaze often centres white, middle-class women.[2] The theoretical female gaze concerns how images are made and by whom; it is not a claim about which male looks women prefer.[2]

subs.h: Two audiences for a man's looks
paras: On looksmax.org the vocabulary appears in thread titles such as 'what does it mean to be male gaze and female gaze', 'definition of the female gaze' and 'height is more male gaze than female gaze'.[8][9][10] Several threads argue that a particular physique or look is 'peak' for one gaze, and some members describe themselves as fitting one or the other.[13][14] Others post a rating-scale argument, for example that a female version of the PSL scale reflects the female gaze and is detached from how women actually rate.[11]

A thread titled 'trying to be a chad is pure male gaze' argues that a conventionally masculine look is aimed at other men's approval rather than at women's.[12] A counterpart thread argues the female gaze favours a softer, 'pretty boy' look.[13] These are positions asserted by forum members rather than measured findings.

Some threads use the pair for women's appearance as well. A looksmax.org thread titled 'Female Gaze vs Male Gaze' posts photos of female models as examples of each, contrasting a high-fashion look with a type the poster says men find attractive.[6] This mirrors the use in cultural criticism, where the male gaze concerns how women are viewed.[1]

Some members regard the female-gaze argument as overstated. A thread titled 'female gaze is cope to an extent' argues that it downplays measurable features, and another with 'pill' in its title treats the female-gaze idea as a source of despair.[7][15] Others argue that the pair describe real differences in what is rewarded socially.[9][13] Wikipedia notes that the blackpill, the ideology that female sexual selection depends mainly on traits such as height and facial attractiveness, has become closely associated with looksmaxxing in mainstream discourse.[4] The female-gaze argument is often set against that view.[4][7]

Scholarly work on the gaze concerns objectification and self-image. Wikipedia reports a 2004 study by Rachel Calogero finding that anticipating the male gaze can increase body shame among college women.[1] A 2017 experiment with 107 women found that, under a male rather than a female experimenter's gaze, women with higher internalisation of beauty ideals showed lower flow and poorer attention performance.[17] A preregistered 2023 experiment with 407 college women found that being video recorded, including with the expectation that men would evaluate the video, raised self-objectification but did not reduce working-memory performance or body satisfaction, and its authors attributed mixed findings in the field to variation in methods.[16] A 2025 paper described how male participants ranked the thinness of composite female body images, torso first, then legs, then arms.[18]

A 2024 study of expert perspectives on weight and visibility used the language of the panopticon and synopticon, ideas about surveillance that echo the gaze literature.[19] These studies concern being looked at, mostly in women, and not preferences for male looks.

subs.h: What studies say about preferences in men
paras: Wikipedia's article on physical attractiveness summarises research on what women tend to prefer in men. Women generally prefer men taller than themselves, with a speed-dating study by Stulp reporting that women were most likely to choose men about 25 cm taller, although some groups, such as the Hadza of Tanzania and rural Gambia, showed no height preference.[5] Women are described as favouring a narrow waist, broad shoulders and a V-shaped torso, a preference for facial symmetry and, on average, for masculine facial features, with preferences varying by cycle phase and by the rater's own attractiveness.[5]

The same article reports that men's magazines show more muscular bodies than women's magazines do, and some researchers have concluded that men's ideal of muscularity is larger than the one women express, which they attribute to competition among men.[5] This literature is cross-cultural, mixed and debated, and it is separate from the forum framework, though it addresses a similar question: whether what men admire differs from what women prefer.[5]

Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing documents coverage by The Conversation, The Guardian, the BBC, The New York Times and The New Yorker between 2023 and 2026, and notes a 2025 study describing a 'hegemonic masculine gaze' on male bodies in the movement. It does not define male and female gaze as looksmaxxing terms.[4] The concept of a female gaze is also discussed in general-interest tech and culture forums, where the theory is debated as a way of looking at the visual arts.[20]

No studies found. Research on the cultural concept of the gaze and on objectification exists, and studies of mate preferences address related questions, but no clinical study has tested the looksmaxxing framework.[16][17][5]

lore.intro: Forum threads treat the two gazes as competing audiences for a man's looks and argue over which should guide self-improvement; some members endorse the split as a planning tool and others dismiss parts of it.[7][8][9]

claims.claim: Height matters more to the male gaze than to the female gaze
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread argues that height is more male gaze than female gaze, meaning other men weight it more than women do.[10]
claims.experts: No study has tested this forum framing. Research summarised by Wikipedia reports that women generally prefer taller men, with a speed-dating study finding a peak near 25 cm taller and some populations showing no height preference.[5]

claims.claim: Female-gaze attractiveness differs from what rating scales measure
claims.believers: Posters argue that the female PSL scale is detached from reality and reflects a particular gaze.[11]
claims.experts: No published studies have compared the PSL scale with women's ratings as the thread describes; Wikipedia calls the PSL scale a forum-created scale.[4]

claims.claim: The female-gaze argument is overstated or a coping narrative
claims.believers: Some members call it a coping narrative that downplays measurable features such as height and bone structure, and tie it to the blackpill.[7][15]
claims.experts: The blackpill idea that female selection depends mainly on physical traits is described by Wikipedia as an ideology of the community; research on mate choice reports that women weigh several traits and that preferences vary by context.[4][5]

claims.claim: A softer 'pretty boy' look is favoured by the female gaze, a hyper-masculine look by the male gaze
claims.believers: Threads argue that conventionally masculine chad traits are aimed at other men's approval, while a softer look draws women's attention.[12][13]
claims.experts: Studies summarised on Wikipedia report that women on average favour masculine facial dimorphism, with preferences varying by menstrual cycle phase and by the rater's own attractiveness, so the research picture is varied.[5]

claims.claim: Muscularity is mostly a male-gaze trait
claims.believers: Posters say that very large muscle mass impresses men more than it draws women, who they say prefer a lean athletic build.[14]
claims.experts: Researchers cited on Wikipedia found that men's magazines show more muscular male bodies than women's magazines and concluded that men see a more muscular ideal than women do; women are described as favouring a V-shaped torso.[5]

claims.claim: Being rated by one gaze makes people self-conscious and affects performance
claims.believers: Members who describe themselves as subject to a gaze say that being judged shapes how they present themselves.[8]
claims.experts: Experiments on women show mixed results: a 2017 study found male-gaze effects on attention for those who internalise beauty ideals, while a 2023 preregistered study found no performance reduction.[16][17]

claims.claim: The same two-gaze logic applies to women's looks
claims.believers: A thread contrasts a high-fashion model type with a type the poster says men find attractive.[6]
claims.experts: A 2025 study of male participants reported that men's rankings of female body thinness focused first on the torso, then legs, then arms.[18]
